## Why Palestinians Hope Israelis Will Oust Netanyahu in Pivotal Election

Many in Gaza and the West Bank are desperate to avoid more years of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing government, which has made life close to unbearable.

Listen

· 10:38 min

![Image 1: One man is carrying a brown box, and another is carrying a white sack on his shoulders as they walk along a dirt street.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/20/multimedia/20int-palestinian-stakes-htlb/20int-palestinian-stakes-htlb-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Palestinians carry food aid from a distribution point in Gaza last month.Credit...Saher Alghorra for The New York Times

Oct. 21, 2026 Updated 9:10 a.m. ET

Israelis have described the election to be held on Oct. 27 as the most important in their history. For Palestinians in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank, the stakes are just as high — even though they do not have a vote.

In previous elections, Palestinians tended to dismiss the candidates to be Israel’s leader as a choice between bad and worse. This time, in the first election since the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, ignited the devastating war in Gaza, many say that replacing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is imperative.

“These elections are existential,” said Nidal Kuhail, 32, a Palestinian who lives in a 6-by-4 meter tent with his three sisters and parents in Gaza after being displaced by the war. “It’s now become a matter of to be or not to be.”

Mr. Netanyahu has vowed to prevent the creation of a Palestinian state, and his government has built Israeli settlements in the West Bank at a breakneck pace.

Image

![Image 2: A man in front of a produce stand with grapes, potatoes and other fruit and vegetables hands money to the seller.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/20/multimedia/20int-palestinian-stakes-04-pbwk/20int-palestinian-stakes-04-pbwk-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Nidal Kuhail at a market in Gaza City in 2024.Credit...Saher Alghorra for The New York Times

Gadi Eisenkot, Mr. Netanyahu’s main opponent, has also rejected Palestinian statehood. But he has promised to curb settler violence in the West Bank and engage with the Trump administration’s cease-fire plan to rebuild Gaza.

The split is one reason Palestinians are paying particular attention to this election, even though their plight is not a major election topic for Israelis in the campaign. In interviews with Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank, they have made clear they do not expect Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents to radically change things for the better. But they are desperate to avoid another four years of Mr. Netanyahu, whose government — the most right-wing since Israel was established in 1948 — has made life almost unbearable.

## Netanyahu’s pressure campaign

In Gaza, the Israeli government has waged a relentless bombing campaign even after reaching a cease-fire with Hamas just over a year ago. Israeli strikes since then have killed more than 1,400 people, according to local health officials, and Israel has [expanded the area of Gaza](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/09/28/world/middleeast/israel-gaza-cease-fire-palestinian-territory.html) it controls. The Israeli military says it is targeting Hamas militants and protecting nearby communities in Israel.

In the West Bank, Israeli settlers have built outposts, harassed Palestinians and set homes and mosques ablaze. Settler [attacks on Palestinians have escalated there during the annual olive harvest of recent weeks](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/world/middleeast/netanyahu-settler-attacks-west-bank-palestinians.html), which is a cultural touchstone for Palestinians and an economic lifeline for many families. On Monday, the Israeli police said they had [detained at least 10 Israelis](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/world/middleeast/israel-west-bank-settlers-palestinians.html) after settlers assaulted Palestinians, along with an American press photographer and European diplomats, during the olive harvest. But the government has largely done little to quell the violence, analysts and rights groups say.

Mr. Netanyahu has occasionally denounced the extremist attackers, but the assaults have continued. He recently hailed the establishment of more than 100 new settlements in the West Bank and pledged that “more were on the way” as part of an effort to entrench Israeli rule across the territory.

Image

![Image 3: A man in a dark suit and blue tie waves his raised hand. He is surrounded by a crowd with many people talking his picture on their phones.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/20/multimedia/20int-palestinian-stakes-01-pbwk/20int-palestinian-stakes-01-pbwk-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with supporters in Yokne’am, Israel on Sunday.Credit...Amir Levy/Getty Images

“This government made a massive effort to realize this generations-old dream,” he told a conference of settlers in August. In the decades since Israel occupied the West Bank in 1967, hundreds of thousands of Israelis have moved there and established communities, widely known as settlements, that are broadly considered illegal under international law.

The Israeli government has also waged economic warfare against the Palestinian Authority, which administers major Palestinian cities in the West Bank. Since the Oct. 7 attacks, the Israeli government has largely banned Palestinians from working in Israel, cutting off a crucial source of income.

The government has also withheld billions of dollars in tax revenue from the Palestinian Authority, after accusing it of using the money to fund terrorism. Palestinian officials deny the accusation.

Mr. Eisenkot has said he broadly supports Israeli settlements. But he has vowed to dismantle any that were built in parts of the West Bank that are supposed to be administered by the Palestinian Authority under the interim peace agreements reached between the Palestine Liberation Organization and Israel in the 1990s.

## The West Bank squeeze

Spurred by Mr. Netanyahu’s far-right allies, Israel has established new settlements in parts of the northern West Bank where Israelis have not lived in recent years. Settlers have also erected many more outposts that are illegal even under Israeli law.

Israeli extremists residing at the outposts have routinely carried out acts of violence — for instance, stealing livestock and cutting down olive trees — which have forced entire communities to flee. In interviews this month, many Palestinian residents said that they hoped a new Israeli government would curb the violence.

Haitham Abdel Jaber, 47, was hospitalized last week with a head injury after settlers assaulted him. Mr. Abdel Jaber, an American citizen, said on Sunday that he was harvesting olives with relatives near his home in Burqa, a village close to Ramallah, when masked assailants hurled stones at them.

Mr. Abdel Jaber said he was hit by a rock while he and his relatives tried to run away. As he was on the ground, he said, his attackers beat and kicked him before fleeing.

The Israeli military said that it sent troops to the area after a report of “friction” between Israelis and Palestinians, including rock throwing.

“We hope Netanyahu loses in the elections,” Mr. Abdel Jaber said. “It’s not that Eisenkot will work for the sake of the Palestinians, but the situation might get better.”

Image

![Image 4: A man in a dark jacket with a furrowed brow stares straight ahead.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/20/multimedia/20int-palestinian-stakes-03-pbwk/20int-palestinian-stakes-03-pbwk-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Gadi Eisenkot, Mr. Netanyahu’s main opponent who was his top general, during a campaign event in Haifa, Israel, last month.Credit...Amit Elkayam for The New York Times

The Israeli economic restrictions have pushed the Palestinian Authority close to bankruptcy.

Nasser Osaily, an entrepreneur active in real estate and importing, said the authority owes him millions of dollars in reimbursements for business he has done with foreign donors. Business owners that occupy stores in his properties, meantime, were struggling to pay rent because Palestinian consumers had little money to spend in them, he added.

“It’s a policy of strangulation. It’s like being grabbed by the neck,” Mr. Osaily said in his office in Hebron.

Bezalel Smotrich, a settler leader now serving as Israel’s finance minister, has urged the next government to crack down even harder. In a [podcast interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zabpzwlXrKc) this month, he said that Israel should “go to war” in the West Bank and do “what we did in Gaza,” a reference to the military campaign that has razed large parts of the enclave.

Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents stress they would seek stability in the territory. Yoram Cohen, who is a senior member of Mr. Eisenkot’s party and a former Israeli intelligence chief, said this would include clamping down on Israeli extremists who attack Palestinians and easing the economic pressure. “We have no interest in igniting a new front,” he said at a party event in Tel Aviv this month.

Palestinian officials in the West Bank, who generally avoid endorsing Israeli candidates, are openly advocating a change of government.

Ukraine says it still doesn’t know why the military satellite internet service, a sister to Starlink, was abruptly throttled, leaving troops vulnerable to Russian attacks.

Listen

· 8:27 min

![Image 1: A figure in camouflage uniform standing in a field and holding a controller, looking up at an airborne drone.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/21/multimedia/21int-ukraine-starshield-01-hglc/21int-ukraine-starshield-01-hglc-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

A Ukrainian soldier flying a drone in the Donetsk region last week. Members of the military have reported issues with drone connectivity since Starshield was disrupted.Credit...Reuters

Oct. 21, 2026, 9:16 a.m. ET

A senior Ukrainian commander said he had dozens of armed drones soaring toward Russian military targets last week when, all at once, the video feeds streaming their flight paths went fuzzy.

The drones had lost their connection to pilots on the ground through [Starshield](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/business/starshield-spacex-ukraine-starlink-satellites-musk.html), a Pentagon-funded satellite internet service, said the commander, Oleh, who spoke on the condition that he be identified by only his first name to protect operational security. Many of the drones simply fell from the sky, he said: The effect cost his units more than $1 million worth of weaponry.

The Starshield disruptions forced Oleh to halt almost all operations for the next three days, he said, including strikes on Russian command posts and fuel hubs. Such attacks, he said, help save the lives of Ukrainian troops holding positions on the front and slow Russian advances.

Ukrainian accounts of Starshield’s abrupt throttling have become a flashpoint in [a worsening feud](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/world/europe/ukraine-war-zelensky-trump.html) between President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine and President Trump. A week after [the first problems](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/world/europe/ukraine-starlink-energy.html) were reported, Ukrainian troops said that the situation had improved but that connectivity issues remained. The Trump administration has [offered mixed messages](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/us/politics/us-intelligence-sharing-ukraine.html), both denying any change to Starshield service and saying that service has been restored.

Ukrainian officials fear that the Trump administration ordered the disruptions to punish Ukraine over its strikes on Russian oil refineries and to force Kyiv to capitulate in the war. Ukraine has also reported gaps in the sharing of U.S. military intelligence and delays in [the delivery of American interceptor missiles](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/06/world/europe/ukraine-russia-missile-defense-patriots.html). U.S. officials deny any such disruptions.

items.title: Shark Returns to Sea After Over a Month Stuck in a South Korean Port Canal
items.summary: The 10-foot-long dusky shark, nicknamed “Bukangi,” was successfully guided back to the open ocean after a third rescue attempt.
items.full_text:
Title: Shark Returns to Sea After Over a Month Stuck in a South Korean Port Canal - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/21/world/asia/south-korea-shark-bukangi-busan.html

Published Time: Wed, 21 Oct 2026 14:00:20 GMT

Markdown Content:
A 10-foot-long shark that became a [celebrity](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/world/asia/south-korea-busan-shark.html) in South Korea after being trapped in a canal in the southeastern city of Busan for more than a month has returned to the open ocean.

Local officials on Wednesday successfully guided the dusky shark, nicknamed “Bukangi,” who had been stuck in the waterway at one of the country’s busiest ports, back into open water, according to a local news network’s [livestream of the effort](https://www.youtube.com/live/QjWDt-En02I). Rescuers attached a wide net to a floating device, which they pulled across the canal using ropes. As the net swept across the water, guiding the shark out, divers made sure it did not get tangled on the canal bed. The process took several hours.

Hundreds of people gathered to watch, with crowds lining both sides of the canal and inching forward as rescuers dragged the net. More tuned in online. “Come back again!” said one online commenter after Bukangi was freed.

The rescue on Wednesday followed two failed attempts. The authorities first tried to guide the shark out of the canal on Sept. 29 using boats and water pumps, but Bukangi dove too far below the surface. The second attempt, on Oct. 2, failed because the rescuers’ net got tangled on the canal bed and the shark managed to swim over it.

The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and the Busan local government were among several agencies that worked on Wednesday’s rescue mission.

Bukangi, who was named by South Koreans after the Bukhang Waterfront Park, where she was trapped, is over 20 years old, experts say. She is the first wild shark to appear in the canal and has become a sensation in South Korea since being first spotted on Sept. 18. Researchers said they were worried because she had not been feeding and would not survive the colder water temperatures in November. Dusky sharks, which live in temperate to tropical waters, can survive up to a month without food.

Over a million people from around the country visited the park to catch a glimpse of the apex predator. The local government has made her an honorary city ambassador.
